claims.text: High-temperature oxidation resistance and material integrity in multiprincipal-element alloys are governed by the formation of a protective oxide scale.
The effectiveness of the protective oxide scale is determined by its oxygen-vacancy concentration.
Al- and Cr-rich alloy compositions promote a continuous, adherent oxide scale with a low oxygen-vacancy concentration.
A low oxygen-vacancy concentration minimizes oxygen diffusivity and reduces oxidation rates.
CoCrFeNiAl and AlxCrFeCoNi are examples of multiprincipal-element alloys that can be prepared by standard casting and homogenization.
Systematic variation of Al and Cr content can control oxide-scale formation.
DFT combined with kinetic Monte Carlo simulation can predict oxygen-vacancy formation and diffusion in candidate oxide phases.
The proposed comparison will test oxidation from 700 to 1000 °C for durations of 100 to 300 hours under controlled oxygen atmospheres.
Oxygen-vacancy concentration in the oxide scale mediates the diffusion of oxygen and metal cations.
An oxide scale with an optimal defect density forms an effective barrier to oxygen ingress.
Sufficient Al and Cr contents facilitate formation of dense, continuous alumina or alumina/chromia scales with low oxygen-vacancy concentrations.
Low oxide defect density limits oxygen diffusion and subsequent oxide growth.
Compositions outside the optimal Al/Cr window form scales with higher oxygen-vacancy concentrations, greater oxygen diffusivity, and faster degradation.
Optimized Al/Cr alloys will have lower oxidation mass gain than lower-Al/Cr baseline alloys.
Optimized Al/Cr alloys will form thinner and more adherent oxide scales and retain better material integrity than the baseline.
Computed higher oxygen-diffusion barriers will correlate with lower experimental oxidation rates.
A lower-Al/Cr baseline is expected to form a porous or poorly adherent scale with higher oxygen-vacancy concentration and accelerated oxidation.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply from 700 to 1000 °C at oxygen partial pressures typical of high-temperature service.
The mechanism may not apply outside the stated temperature range or under drastically different atmospheres.

The hypothesis is falsified if predicted low oxygen-vacancy concentration or high diffusion barriers fail to correlate consistently with lower mass gain, thinner continuous scales, and slower oxidation across the composition series.
